procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated March 25, 1964, terminating the appellant's service under Rule 12 of the M.P. Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition (Misc. Petition No. 272 of 1964) in the Madhya Pradesh High Court to quash the order dated March 25, 1964. The High Court summarily dismissed the petition, holding that the order was not by way of punishment and that the appellant's services were liable to be terminated under Rule 12 on one month's notice. The point that the High Court had recommended the appellant's confirmation was not raised in the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether Rule 12 was unconstitutional as it was framed without consulting the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that Rule 12 was unconstitutional because it was created without consulting the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.
law: A legal argument that raises mixed questions of law and fact cannot be introduced for the first time on appeal to the Supreme Court; it must have been raised in the lower court (the High Court).
application: The Supreme Court categorized the appellant's argument as a "mixed question of law and fact."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, not on its merits, but on procedural grounds, stating that since the issue was not raised in the High Court, it could not be considered for the first time on appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the termination of the appellant's services was punitive and attracted the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant was a temporary government servant in the judicial service.
Complaints were made against the appellant for associating with a girl and taking bribes.
The Chief Justice of the High Court enquired into the complaints and the High Court recommended the termination of the appellant's service.
The State Government issued an order terminating the appellant's services under Rule 12 of the M. P. Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960.
The termination order itself simply stated that the services were terminated and did not mention the complaints or the inquiry.
law: Article 311 of the Constitution provides procedural safeguards to government servants against dismissal or removal by way of punishment.
A termination order in an unexceptionable form, which is preceded by an inquiry only to ascertain if a public servant should be retained in service, does not attract Article 311.
For a termination to be considered punitive, it must cast a stigma on the employee's character or integrity or visit them with evil consequences.

A temporary government servant has no right to hold the office, and their services can be terminated under the applicable service rules without a formal inquiry, provided the termination is not punitive.
application: The Court examined the termination order and found that, on its face, it was a simple order of termination.
The Court held that the order did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity, nor did it result in any 'evil consequences' for him.
The Court characterized the prior inquiry by the High Court not as a formal disciplinary proceeding, but as a process to determine the appellant's suitability to be retained in service.

The Court emphasized the appellant's status as a temporary government servant who had no vested right to the office. Therefore, the government had the right to terminate his services under Rule 12 without providing an opportunity to show cause, as long as the termination was not a punishment.
Since the order was not punitive in nature, the Court found that the procedural protections of Article 311 were not required.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, concluding that the termination of his services was not punitive and did not attract the provisions of Article 311. The Court reasoned that the termination order itself was non-stigmatic and did not entail any evil consequences. The preceding inquiry was merely to assess the appellant's suitability for retention, not a formal disciplinary action. As a temporary servant with no right to the post, his services could be terminated under the rules without the safeguards of Article 311.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's services could be terminated on one month's notice, given that his confirmation was allegedly recommended and the job advertisement did not specify such a termination clause.

facts: The appellant was a temporary government servant whose services were terminated with one month's notice.

The appellant argued the termination was improper for two reasons: (a) the High Court had allegedly recommended his confirmation, and (b) the job advertisement did not mention a one-month termination clause.
law: A point not raised in the High Court cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
The services of a temporary government servant are subject to the relevant service rules.
Under Rule 12 of the M. P. Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960, the services of a temporary government servant can be terminated on one month's notice.
application: The Supreme Court refused to consider the appellant's argument about his recommended confirmation because it had not been raised in the High Court.
The Court found it immaterial that the job advertisement did not specifically mention the termination clause.
The Court determined that the appellant's employment was governed by the applicable service rules, specifically Rule 12, which permitted termination on one month's notice.
The Court also noted that there was no provision in the appellant's appointment order or any other agreement that stated his services could not be terminated in this manner.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's arguments, holding that as a temporary government servant, his services were correctly terminated on one month's notice under the applicable service rules (Rule 12), and the contents of the job advertisement or a newly raised claim about confirmation did not override these rules.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a temporary government servant whose services could be terminated on one month's notice under Rule 12.

facts: The appellant was appointed as a temporary Civil Judge in Madhya Pradesh.
The appellant was not in quasi-permanent service.
There was no provision in the appellant's order of appointment or in any agreement stating that his service could not be terminated on one month's notice.
law: Rule 12 of the Madhya Pradesh Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960, provides that the service of a temporary government servant who is not in quasi-permanent service is liable to termination at any time by one month's notice.
application: The Court determined that the appellant's employment status was that of a temporary government servant, and therefore, his service was subject to the relevant rules, including Rule 12.
The Court rejected the appellant's argument that the job advertisement's failure to mention the possibility of termination was relevant, deeming it "immaterial."

The Court also refused to consider the appellant's point that the High Court had recommended his confirmation, as this argument was not raised in the lower court and could not be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
As a temporary servant, the appellant had no vested right to hold the office, and the state government had the right to terminate his services under Rule 12.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the appellant was a temporary government servant, not in quasi-permanent service, and his services could be legally terminated on one month's notice under Rule 12.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The government can terminate the services of a temporary judicial officer, who has no vested right to the post, based on the recommendation of the High Court, which is constitutionally vested with control over the subordinate judiciary. Such a termination, if it does not cast any stigma or entail punishment, does not attract the procedural protections of Article 311 of the Constitution.
obiter: A contention that raises mixed questions of law and fact cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
It is immaterial that a job advertisement for a government post does not specifically mention that services can be terminated under the relevant service rules.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant was a temporary government servant who had no vested right to hold the office. Therefore, the State government had the right to terminate his services under Rule 12 of the M. P. Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960. As the termination order, on its face, did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity and was not passed by way of punishment, the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution were not attracted, and no opportunity to show cause was required.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a termination order is punitive is determined by its face value; if it does not cast any stigma on the employee's character or integrity or visit him with any evil consequences, it is not considered punishment and does not attract Article 311.
A temporary government servant has no right to hold the office, and their services can be terminated in accordance with the applicable service rules.
Arguments raising mixed questions of law and fact cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court if they were not raised in the High Court.

The provisions of Article 320(3)(c) of the Constitution, regarding consultation with the Public Service Commission, are not mandatory and their absence does not afford a public servant a cause of action.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that Rule 12 was unconstitutional was rejected because it raised mixed questions of law and fact and was not raised in the High Court, so it could not be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
The termination order was not punitive because, on its face, it did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity, and therefore the protections of Article 311 were not attracted.
As a temporary government servant, the appellant had no vested right to the office, and the government was entitled to terminate his services under Rule 12.
The argument that the order was invalid for lack of consultation with the State Public Service Commission failed because the provisions of Article 320(3)(c) are not mandatory.
why_respondent_won: The appellant was a temporary government servant and had no right to hold the office.
The State government had the right to terminate the appellant's services under Rule 12 without issuing any notice to show cause against the proposed action.
The termination order was not passed by way of punishment, as it did not cast any stigma or visit the appellant with any evil consequences.

The government properly acted on the advice of the High Court, which is vested with control over the subordinate judiciary and could properly ask the government to terminate the appellant's services if it found him unfit.
policy_considerations: The High Court is vested with control over the subordinate judiciary. If the High Court finds that a judicial officer is not a fit person to be retained in service, it can properly ask the government to terminate his services.
